summary: An unauthenticated client can force quadratic CPU and allocation work by drip-feeding a chunked HTTP body, because every receive reparses and recopies all previously completed chunks from the beginning before the address allowlist is checked.
evidence: SocketHandlerConnected appends each received fragment to m_recv_buffer and immediately calls MaybeDispatchRequestsFromClient. That function creates a fresh HTTPRequest; ReadRequest constructs a fresh LineReader over the complete buffer and erases nothing until all request components parse successfully. LoadBody creates a new temporary body string, scans every prior chunk, and returns false when the next chunk or delimiter is incomplete, discarding the accumulated copy. Repeating this with many small chunks makes total work grow quadratically up to the 32 MiB body limit. ClientAllowed is only invoked by MaybeDispatchRequestToWorker after the complete request has been parsed, so a source that will ultimately be rejected can still impose this cost when the RPC listener is externally reachable.
context: The per-request body limit bounds one parse but not repeated parsing across receives; each new byte also resets the connection idle timestamp.

summary: An RPC client can grow an unbounded in-memory queue of pipelined HTTP requests while an earlier request is busy, allowing remote memory exhaustion.
evidence: MaybeDispatchRequestsFromClient parses every complete request present in m_recv_buffer and pushes each owning HTTPRequest into m_req_queue, which is an uncapped deque. It checks m_req_busy only after filling the queue and dispatches at most one request. GenerateWaitSockets suppresses receives only while response bytes are pending, not while m_req_busy is true, so the socket handler continues accepting and queueing pipelined requests while a worker handles the prior one. Invalid authentication deliberately occupies a worker for 250 ms before generating a response, providing a simple way to widen the accumulation window; slower valid RPC methods have the same effect. Neither a per-client request-count cap nor an aggregate queued-byte cap constrains this queue.
context: The separate HTTP worker work-queue depth does not bound this per-connection deque because requests accumulate here before being submitted to that queue.
